co2.title: CO2 emissions
co2.explain_p1: The blue curve is what's physically emitted on the country's soil — factories, cars, heating. The dashed orange curve (when available) is what's tied to everything people in the country buy and consume, including goods made elsewhere and imported.
co2.explain_p2: Concrete example: an object made in a factory abroad, then bought and used here. Making it emitted CO2 where the factory is — that CO2 counts in that country's blue curve, not ours, since it wasn't emitted on our soil. But since we're the ones using the object, that CO2 really "belongs" to our consumption — that's what the orange curve tries to capture. If orange is above blue for a country, it means that country buys (and therefore causes emissions elsewhere) more CO2 than it emits itself on its own soil.
co2.explain_p3: Important: neither blue nor orange is "the real one" — both count real CO2 emissions, just with two different rules for deciding who they belong to (where it's produced, or by whom it's consumed). And above all: they're never added together. They're not two pieces of one total — they're two ways of slicing up the same world total of emissions.
co2.chart_label_consumption_total: Tied to what's bought, imports included (Mt CO2)
co2.chart_label_consumption_per_capita: Tied to what's bought, per capita (t)
co2.details_p1: The solid (blue) curve shows territorial emissions ("production-based"): what's physically emitted on the country's soil (factories, transport, heating, agriculture...). It does not include emissions tied to making imported goods — an object made abroad and consumed here counts in the manufacturing country's emissions, not ours. This is the method states use for their international commitments.
co2.details_p2: The dashed (orange) curve, when available, shows "consumption-based" emissions: territorial emissions, minus what's exported, plus what's imported — so it reflects imports. It only exists for some countries (the largest economies, with detailed enough trade data), and always lags one year behind territorial emissions.
co2.details_p3: In both cases, international aviation and shipping emissions aren't counted in any country's figures.
co2.source: Source: Global Carbon Project, via Our World in Data (CC-BY)

eau.title: Water resources
eau.chart_stress: Share of available water actually withdrawn (%)
eau.second_chart_title: This second chart: how much of this water is used?
eau.explain_p1: The chart above shows how much water exists. This one shows how much of that water is withdrawn each year, as a percentage. Example: at 25%, the country uses a quarter of the water that renews each year — three quarters remain. At 120%, the country uses more water than it renews each year: it draws on reserves that don't recharge (deep aquifers) or desalinates seawater to compensate.
eau.explain_p2: Reference thresholds (FAO/UN): below 25%, no water stress at all. Between 25 and 50%, low stress. Between 50 and 75%, medium stress. Between 75 and 100%, high stress. Above 100%, critical stress — the country draws water faster than it renews.
eau.explain_p3: And the water that isn't withdrawn, what happens to it? It's not lost — it simply continues its natural cycle: it flows in rivers (needed for aquatic ecosystems, diluting pollution, navigation), recharges aquifers, evaporates, or reaches the sea. "Withdrawal" only counts water actively extracted for agriculture, industry and households.
eau.details_summary: What exactly do these figures cover?
eau.details_p1: The blue curve shows renewable freshwater resources available per capita (internal rivers, aquifer recharge, plus inflows from neighboring countries) — an indicator of relative water scarcity, not actual consumption. It's a long-term estimate, recalculated each year mainly to account for population changes: the underlying physical resource rarely changes from one year to the next.
eau.details_p2: The dashed green curve shows annual rainfall measured by satellite (Copernicus ERA5 reanalysis) — this genuinely varies each year. For very small countries, this measurement can be less reliable (climate grid resolution).
eau.details_p3: The purple chart shows actual water withdrawals (agricultural, industrial and domestic consumption combined) — the direct comparison with the blue curve: if withdrawals durably exceed renewable resources, it's a sign of reliance on non-renewable aquifers or desalination.
eau.source: Sources: AQUASTAT/FAO via World Bank (renewable resources and withdrawals), Copernicus ERA5 (rainfall), via Our World in Data (CC-BY)

energie.title: Power plants
energie.map_sobriety_disabled: Map disabled in lean mode (saves tile downloads)
energie.no_plants: No power plants found for this filter.
energie.map_explain: This map shows existing power plants and their installed capacity — the maximum power they could produce running flat out all the time. It's not what they actually produce: a 100 MW solar panel produces nothing at night, a 100 MW nuclear plant runs almost all the time. To see actual output, see the chart further down.
energie.mix_summary: {count} production types, {capacity} MW of known total capacity.
energie.mix_explain: Installed capacity by fuel type, with the number of plants — the same chart as on the country page, to find the same information here.
energie.generation_explain: Unlike the map above (installed capacity, fixed since 2021), here's what's actually produced each year, by fuel type — the stacked bars show the real production mix. The dashed black line is actual consumption (demand). Example: if the black line is above the stacked bars, the country imports electricity from its neighbors to make up the shortfall; if it's below, it exports.
energie.generation_source: Source: Ember / Energy Institute, via Our World in Data (CC-BY)
energie.source: Source: Global Power Plant Database, World Resources Institute (CC-BY 4.0) — latest published version (v1.3.0); this project hasn't been actively maintained by WRI since 2021-2022, so the data doesn't necessarily reflect the very latest plants built.
energie.source_refresh: Automatic monthly refresh (no effect unless the source itself is updated).

vegetation.title: Tree cover loss
vegetation.explain_p1: Think of the country's forest as a large reserve. Each year, part of it disappears (cut, burned, cleared) — that's the orange bar, in hectares (1 hectare ≈ 1 football pitch). But the same number of lost hectares doesn't weigh the same depending on the reserve's size: losing 10,000 hectares in a small, heavily forested country is a huge share of its forest; losing the same 10,000 hectares in a huge country like Brazil is almost nothing. The red curve (%) corrects for that: it truly says "what share of its forest the country loses that year".
vegetation.explain_p2: The dashed purple curve shows something else: the loss added up since the first available year, relative to the forest size at that time. Losing 1% a year seems small, but added up over 20 years, it can represent a large part of the original forest — this curve gives the real scale over the whole period covered by the data.
vegetation.note_technical: Technical note: total forest area (FAO) is only measured every few years, while loss is annual. Between two measurements, we use the closest known value rather than leaving the % curves empty.
vegetation.chart_share_year: % of forest cover lost that year
vegetation.cumulative_summary: In total, between {startYear} and {endYear}, {country} lost {totalLoss} ha, or about {percent}% of the forest as it existed in {startYear} (first year with loss data) — this figure keeps growing every year, it never stops.
vegetation.table_caption: Tree cover loss for {country}, by year
vegetation.details_summary: What exactly do these figures cover?
vegetation.details_p1: This is tree cover loss detected by satellite (30m resolution, Hansen et al.), all causes combined — clear-cutting, fire, logging, agriculture. It's not necessarily permanent deforestation: a plot can regrow after managed logging. Loss data covers 2001-2024.
vegetation.details_p2: The red curve (% lost) relates this annual loss to the country's total forest area that year (FAO, recalculated every 5 years and interpolated in between) — to give a relative sense of scale rather than a raw hectare figure with no context.
vegetation.source: Source: Global Forest Watch, via Our World in Data (CC-BY)

especes.title: Threatened species
especes.intro_p1: Sample of species observed in this country, by IUCN extinction category, based on occurrences republished by GBIF. This is not the complete list of assessed species, but a representative sample. Common names with no known translation are shown as such rather than guessed.
especes.intro_p2: Categories go from least to most severe: "Vulnerable" means threatened but not immediate danger, "Endangered" means it could disappear in the medium term without action, and "Critically endangered" means it risks disappearing in the very near future.
especes.no_species: No species found for this filter in this sample.
especes.source: Source: GBIF, occurrences classified by IUCN category via the GBIF-IUCN partnership (CC-BY)
especes.official_count_explain: Unlike the GBIF sample above, this is an official count from IUCN assessments — but limited to just three groups (mammals, birds, fish), and in absolute numbers, not percentages: no source publishes a reliable total of species present per country to calculate a real %.
especes.no_official_data: No official data for this country.
especes.world_reference_explain: For a sense of scale: here's the number and % of species threatened worldwide, by major group (IUCN Red List, via Our World in Data) — this is not specific to {country}. These figures update automatically (open source, legally republished by OWID — the IUCN's own raw data cannot be automatically redistributed under its own terms of use).
especes.world_source: IUCN Red List / UNEP-WCMC via World Bank, via Our World in Data (CC-BY)

incendies.title: Active wildfires
incendies.intro_p1: Satellite detections from the last 3 days (NASA FIRMS, MODIS sensor). A detection isn't necessarily an uncontrolled wildfire — it also includes agricultural burning and other heat sources detected by satellite.
incendies.intro_p2_prefix: Points on the map are colored by the intensity of the heat detected:
incendies.color_yellow_desc: for a moderate detection (often agricultural burning),
incendies.color_red_desc: for the most intense hotspots, more likely to be real wildfires.

pollution.title: Air pollution
pollution.explain_p1: The orange curve is the amount of fine particles breathed on average by the country's inhabitants. The higher it is, the more polluted the air. The green line (5 µg/m³) is the threshold the WHO recommends not exceeding to limit health risks — fewer than 15% of cities worldwide meet it today. Example: a value of 15 µg/m³ means the country breathes, on average, 3 times more fine particles than the WHO recommends.
pollution.details_summary: What exactly does this figure cover?
pollution.details_p1: This is the average annual exposure to fine particles PM2.5, population-weighted (more populated areas count more), estimated by satellite modeling. The WHO recommends staying under 5 µg/m³ to limit cardiovascular and respiratory risks — fewer than 15% of cities worldwide meet this threshold today.
pollution.source: Source: SatPM (Washington University in St. Louis), via Our World in Data (CC-BY)

groupes.title: Political groups — National Assembly (17th term)
groupes.intro: Average voting participation rate by group. Participation says nothing about how they vote — a group can have high participation while voting very differently internally. Factual data, no value judgment.
groupes.chart_alt_participation: Average participation rate by political group
groupes.cohesion_explain: For votes where at least 2 group members cast a vote (for, against, or abstention — absences don't count as disagreement), what share sees the whole group choose the same position. A high figure doesn't mean "better" or "worse" — just more or less internal debate within the group. Calculated over the window of votes with available nominative detail (not the full history).
groupes.chart_cohesion_label: % of votes where the group voted unanimously
groupes.axis_cohesion: % of votes where the whole group voted the same way
groupes.source: Source: CIVIX and National Assembly (official open data) (Licence Ouverte / Open Licence 2.0).
groupes.results_title: Adopted or rejected votes, among those the group participated in
groupes.results_explain: Votes are individual — members of the same group don't always vote the same way. This figure shows, of the {total} votes where at least one group member cast a vote, what share was adopted or rejected by the Assembly — this is not a measure of what the group wanted to achieve.
